terms.definition: a model built from many small parts (neurons) arranged in layers; each part does a little arithmetic and passes its result on.
one small part of a neural network: it multiplies each input by a learned weight, adds them up, and passes the sum through a fixed curve.
a number the network learns; each input is multiplied by its weight, so the weight says how much that input counts.
a group of neurons that work side by side on the same input; a network is several layers, each feeding the next.
one piece of text the model reads: here a single character; later in the chapter a word or a piece of a word.
a list of items where the order matters, like the characters of a sentence.
one position in a sequence; in a character model, one character.
Google's Python library for building and training neural networks; code calls it tf.
the part of TensorFlow used to build networks from ready-made layers, as tf.keras.
a Keras layer that learns a vocabulary from text and then turns text into lists of integer IDs, one per token.
the list of all distinct tokens the model knows, each with its own ID.
filler (ID 0) added to the end of short sequences so that every row of a batch has the same length.
the single ID (1) given to any token that is not in the vocabulary.
a lookup table of descriptions, one row per key, that other tables are joined to.
a meaningless integer ID given to each row of a table, e.g. 0, 1, 2 …
a fixed-length slice of consecutive items, e.g. 101 characters; each window becomes one training example.
in SQL, choosing which columns to keep (SELECT a, b).
TensorFlow's tool for feeding data to training: a Dataset hands out the examples batch by batch.
put the examples in a random order.
a group of examples handed to the model together, e.g. 32 windows. (Not ch02's "batch learning".)
the training method: again and again, nudge every weight a little in the direction that makes the error smaller.
graphics processing unit: a chip that does many multiplications at once, which makes training much faster.
the computer's ordinary processor.
a model trained to predict the next token of a text.
one full pass of training over every training example.
a plot of the validation score after every epoch.
a recurrent neural network that reads text one character at a time and predicts the next character.
recurrent neural network: a network whose layer reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a memory (its state) from each step to the next.
looping back: a recurrent layer feeds what it computed at one step into its work at the next step.
the numbers a recurrent layer carries from one step to the next: its memory.
a network where data flows one way, from inputs to output, with no memory between inputs.
a short list of learned numbers standing in for one token; an Embedding layer is the lookup table holding one such row per token ID.
a list of numbers where every position holds a real value (no mostly-zeros).
gated recurrent unit: a kind of recurrent layer whose memory can last many steps.
an ordinary layer where every input feeds every neuron. (ch02's "dense" was about storing every cell of a table.)
a fixed curve applied to a neuron's sum before it is passed on.
turns a row of scores into positive numbers that add up to 1, so they can be read as probabilities.
a Keras recurrent-layer option: True = give an output at EVERY step; False (default) = only after the last step.
Keras's word for a neuron: a layer with 128 units has 128 neurons.
the one number that says how wrong the predictions are; training changes the weights to make it smaller.
the usual classification loss: small when the model gave the right answer a high probability. "sparse" = the answers are plain IDs, not one-hot rows.
in Keras, fix a model's loss, optimizer and metrics before training.
the algorithm that changes the weights during training, e.g. Adam.
Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts each weight's step size; Nadam is Adam with Nesterov momentum added.
carrying part of the previous weight update into the next one, which smooths training.
in Python, lambda x: … writes a small unnamed function in one line; Keras's Lambda layer wraps such a function as a layer.
the position of the largest value in a list.
how many distinct values a column has; high-cardinality = very many.
running a trained model for real users; "training/serving mismatch" = the two treat data differently.
an object Keras calls at fixed moments during training, e.g. at the start of each epoch.
always choosing the single most probable next token.
drawing items at random; when generating text, drawing the next token at random so that more probable tokens come up more often.
the number the logits are divided by before sampling: low = safe and repetitive, high = wild.
a raw score before it is turned into a probability; here the logarithm of a probability.
always giving the same output for the same input.
keeping the k most probable partial sentences at every step instead of only the best one (b11).
sampling only among the most probable tokens (top k, or those whose probabilities add up to a threshold).
an RNN that keeps its state from one batch to the next instead of resetting it. (ch02's "stateful" meant a Scikit-Learn tool that learns something in fit.)
the normal kind: the state is reset to zeros at the start of every batch.
how a network learns: after a prediction, the error is passed backward through the network to work out how each weight should change.
for one weight, how much and in which direction the loss changes when that weight changes.
updating a table by adding only the new rows on each run.
the saved position (e.g. last timestamp) where the previous incremental load stopped.
one slice of a big table or job that is stored or processed on its own.
how much work gets done per second.
doing several pieces of work at the same time.
deciding whether a text is positive or negative, e.g. a film review.
the Internet Movie Database; its 50,000 labelled film reviews are a standard test set for sentiment analysis.
a library that downloads well-known datasets ready for tf.data (imported as tfds).
cut text into tokens (characters, words or word pieces).
the S-shaped curve that turns any number into a number between 0 and 1.
with two possible values, here 0 (negative) and 1 (positive).
a grid of numbers in rows and columns.
cutting text into word pieces ("smart" + "est") instead of whole words.
byte pair encoding: start from single characters and keep merging the most frequent neighbouring pair into one token.
TextVectorization's learning step: read the text once and build the vocabulary.
the share of examples the model gets right.
marking padding positions so that the layers skip them; the mask is a list of True (real) and False (padding).
True or False.
a model that takes a sequence in and gives a sequence out: in b01 a window of characters in and the next character at every position out; in b08–b12 an English sentence in and a Spanish one out.
the Keras way of wiring layers by calling them on each other's outputs, allowing several inputs.
a layer that slides a small learned pattern-detector along the data; CNN = convolutional neural network.
during training, randomly set some values to 0 so the model cannot lean on any single one.
a table of numbers whose rows have different lengths.
grouping sequences of similar length into the same batch so little padding is needed.
TensorFlow's array: numbers with a fixed shape, e.g. [32, 100].
a single value, not a list.
already trained by someone else, usually on a huge amount of data, and downloaded for reuse.
an embedding for a whole word; Word2vec and GloVe are famous downloadable sets of them.
a large collection of text.
an embedding computed from the whole sentence, so one word gets different numbers in different sentences.
reading a sequence both forwards and backwards.
continuing to train a pretrained model on your own, smaller, labelled task. (In ch02, "fine-tune" meant trying settings.)
training where the labels come from the data itself, e.g. the next word of a text.
the best published result so far.
a website of pretrained models that load into TensorFlow in one line.
a named setting the operating system hands to a running program.
allowed to change during training; trainable=False freezes a layer's weights.
how big each weight update is.
one spelling with several meanings, like "right".
the share of examples the model gets wrong.
translating text from one language to another with a model.
the network that reads the whole input sentence and summarises it.
the network that writes the output sentence, one word at a time, from the encoder's summary.
during training, feeding the decoder the CORRECT previous word instead of its own guess.
using a trained model to make predictions (as opposed to training it).
the known correct answer.
producing a sequence by feeding each output back in as the next input.
long short-term memory: a recurrent layer that carries TWO states, a short-term one (its output) and a long-term one (its memory).
a training shortcut for huge vocabularies: compute the loss from the correct word and a random sample of wrong ones only.
training settling on good weights.
a model is causal if each output depends only on earlier and current inputs, never later ones.
join lists or tables of numbers side by side.
k, the number of partial sentences beam search keeps.
the probability of something GIVEN what came before.
a score for translations: how many word sequences they share with human translations.
a layer that, at each step, scores every position of another sequence, turns the scores into weights with softmax, and returns the weighted sum.
the raw score saying how relevant one encoder output is to the current decoder step.
the numbers that summarise the input sentence for the decoder: in b08–b09 the encoder's final state; with attention (b12), a weighted sum of all the encoder's outputs, recomputed at every step.
multiply two lists of numbers position by position and add the results: one number.
attention works like a lookup: the query is what is being looked for, each key is what a candidate is matched on, each value is what that candidate returns.
the list of steps a database works out before it runs an SQL statement.
has a gradient, so it can be trained by backpropagation.
flip a matrix on its side: rows become columns.
the two classic ways of scoring alignment: a small trainable network (Bahdanau) or a dot product (Luong).
a network built only from attention layers, with no recurrent layers (2017). Not ch02's Scikit-Learn transformer.
a vector added to each token's embedding that says where in the sequence the token sits.
several attention calculations run side by side on different learned views of the same data.
attention where a sequence looks up its own positions: every word scores every other word of the same sentence.
attention where the decoder's queries look up the encoder's keys and values.
a shortcut that adds a layer's input straight onto its output (also called a skip connection).
rescaling the numbers of one token so they average 0 with a typical size of 1.
two wave functions that go smoothly up and down between −1 and +1, a quarter wave apart.
how fast a wave repeats.
NumPy's rule for adding a smaller array to a bigger one by repeating it along the missing axis.
attention whose scores are dot products divided by the square root of the key width.
a learned matrix multiply with no activation function.
a smaller set of directions picked out of a longer vector.
one of the parallel attention calculations in multi-head attention; also the small last layer that gives a model its task ("output head").
when softmax gets huge inputs, one output is almost 1 and the rest almost 0, and learning stalls.
in SQL, a loop that handles one row at a time.
in SQL, one statement that handles all rows together.
a pretrained transformer encoder from Google (2018); DistilBERT is a smaller copy of it.
the pretraining task of guessing hidden (masked) words of a sentence.
the pretraining task of saying whether sentence B really follows sentence A.
an extra vector added to each token saying whether it belongs to sentence A or B.
a transformer that reads an image as a sequence of small square patches.
a small square piece of an image, e.g. 16 × 16 pixels.
an assumption built into a model's design instead of learned from data.
a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears in the image.
one of the colour layers of an image: red, green or blue.
training a new model to copy a strong existing model's outputs.
being able to see why a model gave its answer.
a 2021 DeepMind transformer that reads very long inputs through a small fixed set of latent tokens.
the model's own internal summary vectors.
handling several kinds of input (text, images, sound) in one model.
a company and website hosting thousands of pretrained models; its Python library is called transformers.
the Hugging Face function that downloads a model and runs text through it in one call. Not ch02's Scikit-Learn pipeline.
deciding whether sentence B follows from sentence A (entailment), contradicts it, or neither (neutral).
the tokenizer's list of 1s (real tokens) and 0s (padding).
a saved copy of a model's weights.
a neuron's own extra number, added to its weighted sum; it is learned like a weight, and a layer has one per neuron.
a systematic lean of a model's answers in one direction; in b18, treating some groups of people unfairly because of what was in its training data.
change one attribute of an input (e.g. a country's name) and check the prediction does not change.
a document published with a model saying what it is for and its known limits.

a small state machine (a diagram of states joined by arrows, each arrow labelled with a letter) that decides which letter strings are valid: a string is valid if you can walk it from the start state to the end state; used to test sequence models.
two encoders (e.g. one for images, one for text) trained so that matching pairs get similar vectors.
two early (2018) pretrained language models built from recurrent layers.
a pretrained Google model that turns a whole sentence into one vector of 512 numbers.
writing a text description of an image.
said of languages where one word takes many forms (endings, prefixes).
a name of a person, place or company.
in Python, a blueprint for objects: the data an object holds plus the functions (methods) it can run; a subclass is a class built from another one.
**kwargs collects any extra named arguments so they can be passed on unchanged.
a special value that marks a boundary, like startofseq and endofseq.
another deep-learning library (from Meta), the main alternative to TensorFlow.
